mappings.note: Orion placed in the constellation class is classification of celestial objects, the only astronomy outcome in the frame. Not LO-5, because no phenomenon is explained.
Shooting stars identified as meteors places a familiar sight in its proper class. Not LO-4, because the item names the object rather than asking why it glows.
The farthest planet orders the solar system's members. Not LO-1, since celestial objects are named in LO-2, not in the differentiation outcome.
Converting an age in years into revolutions round the Sun applies an understanding of Earth's revolution, a phenomenon to be explained. Not LO-2, because nothing is being classified.
The least dense planet characterises solar-system members by a property. Not LO-1, whose examples are materials and organisms rather than celestial bodies.
A bright head with a lengthening tail identifies a comet, a celestial object class. Not LO-4, because the tail's growth is described rather than explained.

Shooting stars actually being meteors is the same identification as the earlier item and shares its code, the two being near duplicates. Not LO-5, since the item asks what they are rather than how they form.
Aryabhata as India's first satellite is a landmark story of scientific achievement, which LO-11 covers. Not LO-12, which is used here for what satellites are used for.
Saturn floating on water follows from its density, a property that characterises the planet. Not LO-4, because no observed phenomenon is being traced to a cause.
Why Mars is hard to observe relates an observation to its cause, which is LO-4's pattern. Not LO-2, because the item explains rather than classifies.
Venus not being visible at midnight is explained by its position relative to the Sun, an observation traced to its cause. Not LO-2, since Venus's class is not in question.
Pluto's removal from the planets by the IAU is a reclassification of a celestial object. Not LO-11, because the item asks which body, not the story of the decision.

What a light year is, a unit of distance, is a measurement question, and the frame's only measurement outcome, LO-7, is confined to angles of incidence and reflection. Cited at competency level because no learning outcome reaches it.
Which physical quantity the light year measures is again measurement, with no learning outcome in the frame covering it. Same reasoning as the preceding item.
Naming a star pattern a constellation is classification of celestial objects. Duplicate in substance of the Orion item.

The height of a geostationary satellite belongs to the human use of space technology, which the day-to-day application outcome covers. Not LO-2, because an artificial satellite is not one of the natural celestial classes.
India's first satellite is a milestone story of scientific achievement. Duplicate of the Aryabhata item and coded the same way.
Jupiter as a gas giant assigns a planet to a class. Not LO-1, because celestial objects belong to the classification outcome.
How stars appear to move describes the nightly phenomenon rather than asking its cause. LO-4 was kept for the why-items such as the pole star's stillness.
Placing Orion in its category is classification of celestial objects. Duplicate in substance of the earlier Orion item.
The great red spot identifies Jupiter by a distinguishing feature. Not LO-4, because the spot is not being explained.
Where a spy satellite is deployed is about the human use of artificial satellites. Grouped with the other artificial-satellite items on the application outcome.
Identifying Ceres as a dwarf planet or asteroid is classification of a celestial object. Not LO-11, because no discovery story is told.
The brightest non-star object ranks celestial bodies by appearance. Not LO-5, because no phenomenon is explained.
The only volcanically active moon characterises a celestial object by a distinguishing feature. Not LO-4, since the volcanism is not explained.
The largest natural satellite ranks moons, a class of celestial object. Not LO-12, because artificial satellites are not involved.
Which planets are visible to the naked eye groups celestial objects by observability. Not LO-12, because no instrument or application is chosen.
The shape of the orbits satellites follow describes orbital motion, a phenomenon. Not LO-2, because nothing is placed in a class.
The biggest constellation ranks members of a celestial class. Not LO-11, since no discovery is involved.
Ozone being made of oxygen is the composition of a material, which LO-1 covers through structure. Not LO-2, because one substance is described rather than a set classified.
Who proved planets move in elliptical orbits is a story of scientific discovery. Not LO-5, because the item asks who rather than how the orbits work.
Which planet was farthest during 1979 to 1999 turns on Pluto's crossing orbit, a characteristic of these bodies. Not LO-5, since no motion is explained.
The planet with the longest rotation compares celestial objects on a property. Not LO-5, because rotation is not being explained.
Identifying Halley as a comet places an object in its class. Not LO-11, because the item asks what it is, not who found it.
The Sun's age characterises a celestial object. Not LO-11, since no discoverer or story is involved.
Stars being mostly hydrogen and helium characterises a class of celestial object. Not LO-1, whose examples are terrestrial materials and organisms.
Choosing the correct statement about galaxies tests the properties of that celestial class. Not LO-5, because no phenomenon is explained.
Why the pole star appears fixed relates an observation to Earth's axis, a cause. Deliberately different from the apparent-motion item, which asks what is seen rather than why.
Live telecast made possible by communication satellites is science applied in daily life. Not LO-2, because an artificial satellite is not a natural celestial class.
